prompt: What is wrong with protecting the portal with one excellent control?
hint: What happens on the day it fails?

choices.text: Excellent controls are too expensive for a small shop
choices.why: Cost is not the lesson's objection.

choices.text: It is a single point of failure
choices.why: Right. Every control fails sometimes.

choices.text: Auditors require at least three controls per asset
choices.why: No such rule appears in the lesson.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as it is the best on the market
choices.why: The best control still fails sometimes.

prompt: In the Swiss cheese model, when does an incident happen?

choices.text: When any slice has a hole
choices.why: Every slice has holes; that alone is not an incident.

choices.text: When the first slice fails
choices.why: The next slices can still stop it.

choices.text: When the holes in every slice line up
choices.why: Right. Something passes straight through all of them.

choices.text: When there are fewer than three slices
choices.why: The count matters less than whether the holes line up.

prompt: A firewall allows web traffic to the portal, so it cannot stop an attack sent over the web. Does it still belong in the defence?
hint: Holes do not have to be fixed for the defence to work.

choices.text: No; a control with a known hole is worse than none
choices.why: A layer with a hole is useful if the next layer covers it.

choices.text: Yes, if the application covers what it lets through
choices.why: Right. Neither layer is complete; together they cover more.

choices.text: Yes, because firewalls stop all web attacks
choices.why: The prompt says it does not.

choices.text: No; it should be replaced by a second login
choices.why: The firewall blocks everything that is not the web, which a login does not.

prompt: Besides stopping attacks, what do layers buy a defender against a determined attacker?

choices.text: Time, for detection to notice
choices.why: Right. A log that notices step three gives a chance to stop step four.

choices.text: A lower insurance premium in every case
choices.why: Insurance is not what the lesson discusses.

choices.text: Immunity from zero-day vulnerabilities
choices.why: Layers make a zero-day less decisive, not impossible.

choices.text: Proof for the auditor that the shop is compliant
choices.why: Compliance is a different subject (lesson 13).

prompt: Order these layers from the outside in.
hint: The data is at the centre.
trap: A threat from outside crosses the building and the network before it meets a machine, and the machine before a program.

prompt: Match each control at the shop to its layer.
Why does the lesson call data the layer that travels?
hint: Every other layer protects a place.

choices.text: Because data is sent over the network
choices.why: That is true and not the point: the network is a place too.

choices.text: It is copied to places the other layers do not reach
choices.why: Right. Only controls on the data go with it.

choices.text: Because backups are kept off-site
choices.why: One example of travelling, not the reason.

choices.text: It moves between layers on its own
choices.why: Data moves because people and programs copy it.

prompt: Why does a good design use both outer and inner layers, according to the section on cost?
hint: Shared and coarse; specific and precise.

choices.text: Outer: cheap and coarse; inner: precise and costly
choices.why: Right. Each covers what the other cannot afford to.

choices.text: Outer layers are always free, so they cost nothing to add
choices.why: A firewall costs money; it is shared, not free.

choices.text: Inner layers protect only the data
choices.why: Host and application are inner layers too.

choices.text: Standards require exactly seven layers, one for each ring
choices.why: The seven are a way to list them, not a rule.

prompt: Match each control to its function.
A defence has excellent preventive controls and no detective ones. What happens on the day prevention fails?

choices.text: The corrective controls start automatically
choices.why: Something has to notice before anything corrects.

choices.text: Nothing, because excellent prevention does not fail
choices.why: Every control fails sometimes.

choices.text: It fails silently and nobody notices
choices.why: Right. The attacker past the password is never seen.

choices.text: The deterrent controls take over
choices.why: Deterrence works before an attempt, not after a breach.

prompt: A visitor book at the office door is which kind of control?

choices.text: Technical and preventive
choices.why: Nothing in it is a program, and it stops nobody.

choices.text: Physical and detective
choices.why: Right. It records who came in.

choices.text: Administrative and corrective
choices.why: It restores nothing.

choices.text: Physical and preventive, since the door is locked
choices.why: The lock is the preventive control; the book records.

prompt: An old machine cannot run MFA and will be replaced next year. The shop restricts who can reach it and watches its logins. What is that, and where is it recorded?

choices.text: An acceptance, recorded nowhere since it is temporary
choices.why: Temporary arrangements are exactly what the register records.

choices.text: A compensating control, in the risk register
choices.why: Right. It covers the same weakness another way, for a while.

choices.text: A deterrent control, posted on the machine
choices.why: It does more than discourage.

choices.text: A transfer of the risk to the vendor
choices.why: Nothing was moved to anybody by contract.

prompt: From outside, with no password, the portal answered sign in first. Which layer held?

choices.text: The file permissions on the server
choices.why: The request never got near a file.

choices.text: The log
choices.why: The log records; it did not stop anything.

choices.text: The login
choices.why: Right. Nobody gets in without signing in.

choices.text: The permission check on payslips
choices.why: That comes after somebody has signed in.

prompt: With ana's leaked password, the attacker read ana's payslip and was refused bruno's. What does that show?

choices.text: The leak caused no damage
choices.why: ana's payslip was read; that is the damage it did.

choices.text: Identity and permission are checked separately
choices.why: Right. The second layer held when the first fell.

choices.text: bruno's password is stronger than ana's, so it resisted the attack
choices.why: bruno's password was never involved.

choices.text: The firewall blocked bruno's page before it reached the portal
choices.why: The portal itself answered not yours to read.

prompt: ls -l printed -rw-r----- 1 bruno hr for salaries.csv. Why could the shop account not read it?

choices.text: shop is not bruno and not in hr
choices.why: Right. The last three characters, ---, are for everybody else.

choices.text: The file is encrypted
choices.why: Nothing in the capture says so; the refusal is the operating system's.

choices.text: The portal was not running
choices.why: cat was run directly, not through the portal.

choices.text: Only root may read files in /srv
choices.why: bruno and the hr group may read this one.

prompt: No layer was breached, yet the log matters most in this test. Why?
hint: Look at the second and third lines.

choices.text: It proves the attack failed
choices.why: ana's payslip was read; and failing is not the news.

choices.text: It records ana's password used from outside the office for another person's payslip
choices.why: Right. That is evidence the password is in the wrong hands.

choices.text: Logs block repeated requests automatically
choices.why: A log records; it blocks nothing.

choices.text: It shows which file the attacker tried to read
choices.why: The file test was the administrator's, not in the portal's log.

prompt: Match each arrangement to the shared cause that makes two layers one.

pairs.left: the portal and the server's admin account share a password
two firewalls from one vendor, same version
the portal and the database trust anything from the office
one administrator writes and approves the firewall's rules

prompt: What makes two controls two layers rather than one?

choices.text: They come from different vendors
choices.why: Different vendors help, and they can still share a password.

choices.text: They fail for different reasons
choices.why: Right. One cause must not defeat both.

choices.text: They sit in different rooms
choices.why: Location is one kind of difference among several.

choices.text: They were bought in different years
choices.why: Age says nothing about shared causes.

prompt: Why does the lesson say more layers is not always better?

choices.text: Attackers prefer targets with many layers
choices.why: Nothing suggests that.

choices.text: Each layer needs upkeep, and contradictions become holes
choices.why: Right. A layer nobody maintains decays into a hole.

choices.text: Standards cap the number of layers at four for a business this size
choices.why: Four is how many the lab portal has, not a limit.

choices.text: Each extra layer halves availability
choices.why: Layers cost something, not a fixed half.

prompt: Several controls in sequence, each able to stop what got past the previous one, is called defence in ___.
In the lab test, which layers stopped or recorded the attacker holding ana's leaked password? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the permission check on payslips
choices.why: It refused bruno's payslip.

choices.text: the portal's log
choices.why: It recorded every request.

choices.text: the login
choices.why: The leaked password passed it.

choices.text: a firewall rule
choices.why: There was none in this test; lesson 5 writes them.
